discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: Cold front has moved east of the Cascades early this morning. Cool upper level trough remaining offshore through Monday before moving inland Monday night. Next system moving southeast Tuesday will move inland Wednesday south of the area. Short blocked upper level pattern Wednesday night through Friday giving Western Washington a dry spell. Next system weakening as it approaches Saturday.
hydrology: The post frontal band of showers is still producing significant rain amounts over the south slopes of the Olympics. In the 3 hour period between midnight and 3 AM rainfall totals in this area have been in the 0.30 to 0.60 inch range. Heavier showers will be coming to an end this morning. The Skokomish River near Potlatch is three tenths of a foot below flood stage right now. This last shot of rain will push the river just over flood stage later this morning. A flood warning is already out and will continue for the Skokomish. The river will recede back below flood stage late today or early Monday. The river will remain below flood stage for the remainder of the week.
River flooding not expected on the remainder of the rivers in the area for the next 7 days. Felton

sections.title: Short term (today through Tuesday)
paragraphs: Satellite imagery and surface observations show cold front has moved east of the Cascades early this morning. Doppler radar has a line of post frontal showers between the coast and Puget Sound at 3 AM/11Z. Temperatures even with the frontal passage were still in the upper 40s to mid 50s.

Band moving through early this morning will be the most organized shower activity of the day. Satellite imagery shows plenty of cold cu off the coast but the parent low associated with the trough is moving north northwest towards the Gulf of Alaska. This will pull the coldest post frontal air northwest of the area through Monday. Air mass somewhat unstable so showers remaining in the forecast with the highest pops along the coast. Snow levels near 5000 feet only lowering to 3500 to 4000 feet by Monday. A few inches of new snow in the higher elevations today but by the time the snow levels drop down to the pass levels new snow accumulations will be light. High temperatures today, in the lower to mid 50s, could occur this morning with little change in the temperatures throughout the day. A little cooler Monday with highs a couple of degrees either side of 50. Lows tonight in the mid 30s to lower 40s.

A coastal flood advisory remains in effect for the Northern Inland Waters this morning between 8 am and noon for possible minor coastal flooding with the combination of high tides, lower surface pressure and winds.

Current wave forecasts are a little lower than previous forecasts for later today into Monday morning. Have cancelled the high surf warning for the beaches beginning at 10 am this morning and extended the high surf advisory through Monday morning. The beaches will still be a dangerous place to be even with an advisory. Still could see waves in the 20 foot range into Monday morning.

Upper level trough moving through the area Monday night keeping a chance of showers in the forecast. Snow levels 3500 to 4000 feet but not much in the way of moisture with the trough passage. Lows in the lower 30s to lower 40s.

Split flow aloft Tuesday with the next system digging south well off the coast giving Western Washington a dry day. Light surface gradients in the morning could produce areas of low clouds or fog. Even with some afternoon sunshine highs remaining near 50.

sections.title: Long term (Tuesday night through Saturday)
paragraphs: Models in good agreement with the mid week system moving inland south of the area. The Southwest Interior could get brushed by the northern portion of the system Wednesday. Short lived upper level blocking pattern setting up Wednesday night through Friday with an upper level ridge to the north and an upper level low to the south keeping Western Washington dry. If the models light surface gradient scenario works out there could be areas of fog Thursday and Friday morning.
Model solutions showing more variability Saturday as the next system develops off the coast. No real clear winner in the ensembles so for now will go with a broadbrush chance of rain.
Highs staying around 50 through the period. Lows in the 30s and lower 40s cooling to the upper 20s and 30s Thursday through Saturday.

The first two weeks of November have been quite mild. For Seattle the average temperature of 51.6 is the 5th warmest in 82 years of records at Seattle-Tacoma airport. Saturday was the 6th day of the month with a high in the 60s. Only three Novembers have had more 60 degree plus days, 2016 with 9 days, 1976 with 8 days and 1949 with 7 days. With the 3 am temperature of 55 degrees this makes the 13th day in a row with a high of at least 55 degrees in Seattle. This is the longest streak of its kind. The previous longest, two 12 days streaks November 1-12, 2016 and November 3-14, 1949. Felton

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: A strong front has moved through the area with southwest winds aloft. Can't rule out a brief period of MVFR cigs under heavier showers today otherwise ceilings look to remain VFR. There is a low (15-20%) chance of isolated thunderstorms, mainly along the coast this afternoon. Breezy winds are to remain today with continued gusts of 15-25 kt before gradually decreasing tonight. Can't rule out gusts near 30 kt for KBLI.

KSEA...VFR throughout the period. Surface winds southerly but could sway between the SW and SE at times. Winds mainly 8-12 kt before gradually decreasing to 3-6 kt later tonight. Can't rule out isolated gusts near 20 kt this afternoon.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A vigorous front has pushed east of the waters but elevated winds and seas will remain today. The previous Storm Force warning for the coastal waters has expired. Any lingering Gale Warnings will be allowed to expire later this morning but SCAs will remain throughout the day for both inner and outer waters. Winds will gradually ease over the waters and later tonight. Waves 15-18 ft this morning will rise to 20-25 ft this afternoon with the highest waves over the offshore waters. High pressure is still on track to build across the area on Monday allowing for a brief reprieve. Winds are to be generally benign as seas lower to 10-12 ft, still SCA for the coastal waters but much lower than we've seen recently.

A low pressure system will form over the open northeast Pacific and move off south and away from WA's coastal waters Tuesday into Wednesday before tracking into CA later on Wednesday. While somewhat distant, this system will allow winds to turn offshore and increase, as well as increasing waves for the next round of headlines mid- week. Calmer conditions under high pressure are then favored Thursday into the end of the week.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: Unsettled showery weather lingers through Monday while a high surf and sneaker waves threat persists across our beaches - the product of the active pattern we've seen the last several days. Snow levels drop to 4000 ft in the Cascades tonight into Monday before conditions quickly trend drier Tuesday. We'll still need to watch for some limited pass snowfall concerns on Wednesday (mainly central OR Cascades) before dry conditions return again to end the week.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Unsettled showery weather lingers through Monday while a high surf and sneaker waves threat persists across our beaches - the product of the active pattern we've seen the last several days. Snow levels drop to 4000 ft in the Cascades tonight into Monday before conditions quickly trend drier Tuesday. We'll still need to watch for some limited pass snowfall concerns on Wednesday (mainly central OR Cascades) before dry conditions return again to end the week.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Saturday...Yet another frontal system has passed through the region early this morning with bands of showers currently spread across southwest Washington and Western Oregon. We'll stay in this post-frontal airmass into Monday. It's worth quickly noting while some of these cells are presenting decently on radar to start the day, model soundings show the CAPE fueling these cells largely below the temperature layer (-10 to -20c) typically needed for electrification. Thus, the probability for T-storms today is low, only around a ~10% chance, but strong cells could still produce heavy rainfall and locally gusty outflow winds. Cooler air gradually filters in aloft over the next 24 hours, allowing snow levels to drop from 6000-7000 ft early this morning to around 4000-4500 ft tonight into Monday morning. Snow showers may occur down to pass level in the Cascades, but probabilities for 2 inch of accumulation or more at pass level remain fairly low (10-35% or less) through Monday morning. By Monday evening, the upper level trough becomes stretched and elongated offshore, pushing south of California before sliding inland across the West Coast and spelling the end for any lingering showers come sunset.

Ensemble members show increasing confidence in a brief break in the active weather pattern Monday night through Tuesday afternoon thanks to a weak transient ridge of high pressure passing overhead. Areas of morning valley fog likely make a return. The next weather system is then slated to approach the PacNW coast late Tuesday into Wednesday, with ensemble clusters now showing better agreement on the general track of this system. Exploring the latest 00/06z guidance, the vast majority of models show the vertically stacked low pressure undercutting us to the south and diving into California. Still, a shortwave rotating around the larger circulation associated with this system will attempt to sling-shot northward into the region increasing chances for precipitation. While precipitation amounts don't appear particularly noteworthy, the airmass will still be on the cooler side when this system hits, and snow levels are forecast to be around 3000-3500 ft Tuesday night into Wednesday. The best chances (30-50%) for 2+ inches will the across the southern portion of our CWA across Santiam and Willamette pass. Otherwise, once we get into the Thursday through Saturday time period, there is good ensemble agreement in prevailing dry conditions with near normal temperatures, enjoy the dry window while we have it. -99/DH

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 12Z Monday...The region remains under scattered post-frontal showers early this morning with mainly VFR conditions in place inland due to an offshore component to the surface flow. Still, KONP has seen a mix of MVFR to LIFR due to degraded CIGS - gradual improvement is to mainly MVFR/VFR is anticipated there this morning. For our other terminals, hourly chances for MVFR conditions hold around 20-35%, mainly associated with the aforementioned shower activity. However, along the I-5 corridor showers likely become more hit or miss late morning into the early afternoon before a brief uptick in activity roughly 22-03z. From 03z onwards showers become more sparse the rest of the TAF period. Again, at any point if a shower moves directly over a terminal brief MVFR conditions are likely. Winds stay a little breezy out of the south today with gusts around 15-25 kts for most sites before decreasing this evening.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...Showers this morning will continue to bounce CIGs/VIS between high-end MVFR and VFR with this trend persisting through the day - most hours should remain VFR. Winds remain southerly, decreasing a touch after 02-03z. -99

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: An aggravated seas state continues into early next week as an yet another frontal system and reinforcing swell takes aim at the region. Our latest frontal system has passed to the east early this morning with seas holding in the mid to upper teens at 12-15 seconds through a good chunk of the daytime hours - a Hazardous Seas Warning remains in effect. As alluded to, a trailing westerly well is expected to arrive late this afternoon and evening, likely pushing significant waves heights back into the 19-23ft range overnight into early Monday morning. Fortunately after this point seas are forecast to gradually diminish below 20 ft by midday Monday, bottoming out near 10-14 ft by Tuesday morning while wind gusts decrease below 20 kts as well. However the lull is fairly short-lived as another frontal system will increase winds again Tuesday afternoon through Tuesday night. There's a 60-80% chance of Gales for locations beyond 30 NM from the coast during this time and a 30-50% chance for the waters within 30 NM from the coast. Another increasing fresh westerly swell follows Wednesday morning, increasing seas to around 14-18 ft at 14-16 seconds through Wednesday night. Looking further ahead, there is decent model agreement for seas to slowly decrease through the end of the week into the first half of next weekend, likely dropping below 10 ft by Friday as the weather pattern briefly calms. Ensemble models hint at another storm system around the second half of next weekend which would bring renewed winds and swells. -99/03

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: Hazardous high surf conditions persist the latter half of the weekend into early next week along the Oregon and southern Washington beaches. Seas currently sit in the upper teens this morning with another westerly swell around 17-22 ft accompanied by a dominant wave periods of 15-18 seconds slated to arrive this afternoon through Monday. This will translate to breakers up to 25 to 30 ft for our beaches. Thus, a High Surf Advisory is in effect through 10 AM Monday before the seas slowly diminish. In these conditions, wave will run significantly farther up on area beaches and jetties than what is normally observed. More simply put, the sneaker wave threat will be very high. Beachgoers should use extreme caution as sneaker waves can suddenly knock people off of their feet and quickly pull them into the frigid ocean which may lead to serious injury or drowning. Never turn your back to the ocean. In addition, large wave runup may dislodge logs on area beaches and result in them rolling up and down area beaches, which have historically killed or seriously injured unsuspecting people, so there will be much more of a threat than just getting wet from a rogue wave. Further beach erosion is also possible. Avoid the beaches if you can.
